content: The DECIDE framework, an evidence-to-decision tool, was utilized to guide the formulation of recommendations. This framework incorporates various criteria, including intervention effects, values, resources, equity, acceptability, and feasibility. The members of the guideline development group, along with their areas of expertise, are detailed in Annex 5. An external resource group, consisting of nine individuals selected by the steering group, provided critical insights to the guideline development group on relevant issues. Their expertise spanned bioethics, hygiene and sanitation, costing and cost analyses, economics, infectious disease epidemiology, reproductive health, and HIV/AIDS. These external experts contributed during open sessions of group discussions but were not involved in the closed-session deliberations where decisions on the wording, direction, or strength of recommendations were made. The members of this external resource group are listed in Annex 6. Systematic review teams were commissioned to address key questions identified during the guideline development group’s scoping meeting. These teams included the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group (focused on deworming in children), the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group (focused on deworming during pregnancy), the Cochrane HIV/AIDS Group (focused on deworming in populations living with HIV), and the Campbell Collaboration (focused on externalities and synergistic effects with co-interventions, including quasi-experimental studies for deworming in children, and deworming in non-pregnant adolescent girls and adult women). These teams provided comprehensive, objective syntheses of evidence, assessed the quality of the evidence, and developed GRADE evidence profiles. Their systematic reviews were presented at the guideline development group meeting in Geneva in April 2016. The members of these systematic review teams are also listed in Annex 6. The steering group managed potential conflicts of interest in compliance with WHO guidelines and in collaboration with the Office of Compliance and Risk Management and Ethics. All potential guideline development group members were required to complete and sign standard WHO declaration-of-interest and confidentiality forms, as well as provide updated curricula vitae. These declarations were reviewed alongside the CVs, and additional information was gathered from public sources to identify any intellectual biases. All concerns were addressed on a case-by-case basis, and members with no perceived or real conflicts of interest were asked to verbally declare their research and funding sources during the meeting. Members with declared interests that warranted conditional participation disclosed their interests publicly at the start of the meeting and in the guideline document. Priority questions and outcomes were identified to guide the formulation of recommendations. These questions were drafted by technical staff based on the policy and programmatic needs of Member States and their partners, then reviewed and finalized by the steering group and the guideline development group. The group ranked the importance of outcomes on a scale from 1 to 9, with higher scores indicating critical importance for decision-making. The final key questions and critical outcomes are presented in PICO format in Annex 1. Evidence identification and retrieval included updates to previous Cochrane reviews on the effects of deworming medicines on nutritional outcomes in children, as well as new trials published since the last systematic review. These included a large trial with over one million participants and a replicated trial from Kenya. Additional systematic reviews were commissioned to address the impact of deworming on pregnant women, non-pregnant adolescent girls, and adult women, as well as the effects of deworming in individuals co-infected with HIV and helminths. The Campbell Collaboration conducted a review to assess the synergistic effects of co-interventions and potential confounding factors. Systematic reviews were conducted following Cochrane Handbook procedures, with each study assessed for risk of bias. The quality of evidence was evaluated based on criteria such as risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, indirectness, and publication bias. Evidence profiles were prepared using the GRADE approach, and the quality of evidence for each outcome was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low. These findings were presented to the guideline development group, along with confidence assessments in the effect estimates for critical outcomes. Draft recommendations were discussed during a meeting of the steering group and the guideline development group in Geneva in April 2016. Three types of recommendations were considered: strong recommendations, conditional recommendations (applicable only in specific contexts), and not recommended. The DECIDE framework was used to guide discussions and decision-making, with domains such as quality of evidence, balance of benefits and harms, and other factors considered. The quality of evidence across critical outcomes influenced the strength of recommendations, with higher-quality evidence supporting stronger recommendations. Conditional recommendations were more likely when evidence quality was low or very low, or when uncertainty existed regarding the net benefits or harms of an intervention.
